name: Norte Chico (Caral-Supe)
summary: The oldest known civilization in the Americas. Emerged along coastal Peruvian rivers with monumental platform pyramids, sunken circular plazas, cotton fishing-net trade, and early quipu knot records—notably without ceramics or fortifications.
keyFacts: Monumental terraced pyramids at Caral contemporary with Egyptian Old Kingdom
Bone flutes and coastal-inland cotton-for-anchovy exchange

name: Chavín Culture
summary: Unifying artistic and religious horizon in the northern Andean highlands. Famous for the labyrinthine stone temple at Chavín de Huántar, the Lanzón monolith, acoustic water drainage, and gold metallurgy.
keyFacts: Lanzón granite monolith and tenon heads
Acoustic temple engineering simulating jaguar roars

name: Nazca & Moche Cultures
summary: While the Nazca on the arid south coast etched giant desert geoglyphs and built underground puquio aqueducts, the Moche in the north built colossal adobe pyramids, irrigation canals, and lifelike portrait ceramics.
keyFacts: Nazca Lines geoglyphs and subterranean puquio aqueducts
Huaca del Sol (largest pre-Columbian adobe structure) & Royal Tombs of Sipán
Masterful Moche stirrup-spout portrait vessels and tumbaga gold alloy

name: Wari & Tiwanaku Empires
summary: Twin highland empires that pioneered state road networks, terraced hillside farming (andenes), raised-field agriculture (suka kollus) around Lake Titicaca, and administrative khipu accounting.
keyFacts: Gate of the Sun & Kalasasaya monolithic architecture at Tiwanaku
Wari highway network and terraced agricultural engineering later adopted by the Inca

name: Kingdom of Chimor
summary: Ruled the northern Peruvian coast from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, renowned for split-inheritance royal compounds (ciudadelas) and industrial-scale gold/silver metallurgy.
keyFacts: Chan Chan adobe metropolis covering 20 sq km

name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
summary: The largest empire in pre-Columbian America, stretching 4,000 km along the Andes. Governed without money or wheeled vehicles through the mit’a labor tax, state granaries (qullqa), quipu registries, and the 40,000 km Qhapaq Ñan road network.
keyFacts: 40,000 km Qhapaq Ñan mountain highway and suspension bridges
Earthquake-resistant ashlar masonry at Cusco, Ollantaytambo, and Machu Picchu
Freeze-dried food preservation (chuño) and high-altitude agricultural laboratories (Moray)

name: Viceroyalty of Peru → Modern Andes
summary: Following Pizarro’s conquest, Peru and Upper Peru (Potosí) became the silver heart of the Spanish Empire before winning independence in the 1820s as Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, and Chile.
keyFacts: Potosí silver mint powering global trade from Seville to Ming China
